Hong Kong: Xiaomi jumps 8% despite profit falling by two-thirds, Asian stock markets rebound on Thursday, led by Seoul

Chinese smartphone maker Xiaomi saw its shares climb as much as 8.2% on Wednesday, November 25 in Hong Kong: its phone sales held up better than expected, even though its profit fell 68%. On Thursday, Asian stock markets rebounded with tech, despite an interest rate hike in South Korea [1][2][4].
In the third quarter (July-September), Xiaomi's revenue fell 5.2% to 107.2 billion yuan, better than the 6% decline analysts expected [1].
Its smartphone sales were flat, while analysts had forecast a 6% decline [1].
Net profit, however, plunged 68% to 3.9 billion yuan [1].
According to Citi, adjusted net profit (excluding one-off items) was broadly in line with expectations; the bank kept its price target at 33.2 Hong Kong dollars [2].
The stock rose as much as 8.2% intraday on Wednesday, its biggest gain in nearly three weeks [1][2]. Two days earlier, on Monday, November 23, it had lost 3.7% [3].

On Thursday, November 26, Asia-Pacific stock markets rose in the wake of Wall Street, where tech stocks rebounded after the previous day's fall [4][5]. Seoul led the gains, and the Korean small-cap index, the Kosdaq, rose 2.32% [4].
The same day, the Bank of Korea raised its key interest rate to 3.25%, its highest level in two years [4].

Key takeaway: on the stock market, what matters is not the raw figure but the gap with what was expected. Investors feared a plunge in Xiaomi's smartphone sales; they are holding up [1]. That relief outweighs a profit cut by two-thirds.

Chinese tech is coming out of a very tough period. On November 19, Alibaba announced a 53% increase in its cloud revenue (remote computing, boosted by AI), but profits below expectations [6]. Its stock lost 1.26% that day [7] and is down about 40% since January [8]. Investors are wary of the billions poured into AI: Alibaba increased its capital spending by 60%, to 50.5 billion yuan, and burned through 34.5 billion yuan of cash in the quarter [7].

Thursday's rebound remains cautious. According to CNBC, investors are still worried about how AI investments are being financed and about new US tariffs [4]. The rate hike decided in Seoul also makes borrowing more expensive for Korean companies and households [4], which could hold back the stock market in the medium term.

Xiaomi is a brand you come across in France, from phones to e-scooters: its results show whether smartphone demand is holding up in China. If you have an “emerging markets” or “Asia” fund in your life insurance savings plan or your PEA, big Chinese stocks like Xiaomi and Alibaba often carry significant weight in it: their roller-coaster ride shows up on your statement.

How it works: the consensus, the bar a company has to clear

Before each earnings release, bank analysts make their forecasts; their average is called the consensus. The share price already reflects these forecasts. For Xiaomi, the market expected a 6% drop in smartphone sales; they were flat [1]. Even with net profit down 68% [1], the surprise is positive, so the stock goes up. The opposite happens too: Alibaba announced 53% growth in the cloud, but profits below expectations, and its stock fell [6][7]. What moves the price is the difference between reality and what everyone already believed.

news.2026-11-26-deere-previsions-2027.ti: Tractors: Deere expects another tough year in 2027, its stock plunges before the open then rebounds on Wall Street
news.2026-11-26-deere-previsions-2027.su: US farm equipment giant Deere released its annual results on Wednesday, November 25. It forecasts 2027 net income of 4.5 to 5.25 billion dollars, well below the expected 5.91 billion. Its stock fell before the open, then recovered: the market is betting on the end of the farm downturn [1][3][6][7].
news.2026-11-26-deere-previsions-2027.po: In the fourth quarter of its fiscal year (August-October 2026), Deere earned 3.89 dollars per share, versus 4.03 dollars expected according to FactSet [2]. Its revenue, 12.1 billion dollars, beat forecasts [2] while falling about 2% year on year [1].
For fiscal 2026, net income reached 4.86 billion dollars, compared with 5.03 billion in 2025 [1][12].
Large farm machinery (“production and precision agriculture”) fell 15% in the quarter, while small agriculture and turf rose 10% and construction 12% [1].

For 2027, Deere is targeting 4.5 to 5.25 billion dollars in net income, below the LSEG consensus of 5.91 billion cited by Reuters [3][4]. This forecast includes a one-off pension charge of 250 to 400 million dollars, which involves no cash outflow [3].
Tariffs are costly: more than 1.1 billion dollars in direct costs in 2026 before refunds, and a net impact of about −300 million expected in 2027 [5].
CEO John May sees “early signs of improvement in large agriculture, led by North America,” but a sector that will still be sluggish in 2027 [5].
The stock lost nearly 5% before the open [7], with CNBC listing it among the day's decliners [13], then was up 3% at midday [7] and more than 2% according to Benzinga [6].
news.2026-11-26-deere-previsions-2027.wh: Key takeaway: Deere is a barometer of American agriculture. When farmers earn less, they postpone buying tractors, hence the 15% drop in large machinery [1]. A year ago, Deere was already saying: “We believe 2026 will mark the bottom of the large agriculture cycle” [9]. The trough is still there, and the recovery expected in 2027 remains modest.

Donald Trump's trade policy weighs on two fronts. First, on Deere's costs: more than a billion dollars in direct tariffs in 2026 [5]. Second, on its customers: China had promised to buy 17 billion dollars of US farm products this year, a promise seen as uncertain as Trump proposes new tariffs against China, the EU and other partners [7]. Fewer exports mean less income for farmers, and therefore fewer tractors sold.

Why did the stock bounce back? Part of the gap comes from the pension charge, which is purely an accounting item [3]. And the bank Baird sees upside if farmers' margins improve, while noting that the share price may already reflect much of the recovery [8].
news.2026-11-26-deere-previsions-2027.fo: Deere is not listed in Paris, but it is held in the US or global equity funds that many French people own through a PEA or a life insurance savings plan. Its figures also reflect the state of global agriculture: when American farmers struggle, competition gets tougher for European farmers in big markets like China.

The reported quarter is already in the past; a share price mainly reflects future profits. When Deere announces 4.5 to 5.25 billion dollars for 2027, versus 5.91 billion expected [3], analysts have to lower their estimates: the stock first falls before the open [7]. Then investors read the details. Part of the gap comes from a pension charge of 250 to 400 million dollars that costs no actual cash [3]. And the boss mentions early signs of recovery [5]. A stock often anticipates the turn of a cycle before it shows up in the accounts: if 2026 is the trough, buyers come back as soon as the worst seems known.

A disappointing forecast can lift the stock if the market sees it as cautious.

Mali: a year after making peace with the junta, gold giant Barrick's new international chief received in Bamako, ahead of a visit to the Loulo-Gounkoto mine

On Wednesday, November 25, Sebastiaan Bock, the new CEO of Barrick International, was received in Bamako by Malian Prime Minister Abdoulaye Maïga. It is the first visit by an executive of the Canadian mining group since the November 2025 agreement, which ended a two-year standoff over the country's largest gold complex [1][3].

Sebastiaan Bock, recently appointed head of Barrick International, arrived in Bamako on Tuesday and met the Prime Minister on Wednesday, according to Investing.com [1][2]. He is due to visit the Loulo-Gounkoto complex on Thursday and Friday, according to a source familiar with the matter [1].
He gave assurances that Barrick is committed to complying with Mali's new mining code, adopted in 2023, which the group accepted in the 2025 agreement [1][5].
Loulo-Gounkoto is Mali's largest gold producer and one of Barrick's most profitable mines [1].

To settle the dispute, Barrick agreed to pay about 430 million dollars, or 244 billion CFA francs, according to Bloomberg as cited by Mining.com; neither the group nor the government has officially published these amounts [4].

In exchange, Bamako released four Barrick employees who had been detained for about a year, and all proceedings against the group were dropped [6]. Barrick regained control of the site in December 2025, with the return of about three tonnes of seized gold [5].
Barrick also withdrew its complaint before ICSID, the World Bank's arbitration tribunal, and Mali renewed the Loulo mine's permit for ten years [5][7].
Barrick is targeting between 260,000 and 290,000 ounces of gold (1 ounce = 31.1 grams) for its share of Loulo-Gounkoto in 2026, compared with 29,000 in 2025, the year of the shutdown [8].

Key takeaway: the visit shows that the relationship between Barrick and Mali's junta has normalized. But production remains below its pre-dispute level, and the group has to live with tougher rules [8][1].

Between 2023 and 2025, the military rulers in Bamako clashed with Barrick over profit sharing and control of the complex [1]. They seized gold, arrested employees and placed the mine under provisional administration, which brought it to a halt [5][6].

At the same time, the country is in the middle of a war. In April 2026, the jihadist group JNIM, linked to Al-Qaeda, announced a “total siege” of Bamako [10], and already claimed to control Kidal, in the north, while targeting Gao, Timbuktu and Ménaka [9].

What happens next will be decided on the ground: the Gounkoto mine has opened a new underground gallery to extend its life, and production in the first half of 2026 exceeded internal targets, according to Africa.com [8]. It remains to be seen whether security will allow this pace to be maintained [9][10].

Gold is at the heart of your savings even if you don't see it: central banks and investors buy it when the world is worried. The Malian case shows the other side of the yellow metal: producing countries want a bigger share, and foreign mining groups have to accept it to stay.

Inflation at 3.8% in the United States: the Fed will almost certainly raise rates on December 9, Wall Street plunges then erases its losses before Thanksgiving

On Wednesday, November 25, the Federal Reserve's (Fed) preferred price index, the PCE, rose to 3.8% year on year in October. Markets now see a rate hike on December 9 as virtually certain. Wall Street first fell, before the Dow Jones ended up 0.33%, at 50,182.95 points [1][2][3].
The PCE measures changes in the prices of what American households consume. It rose from 3.7% in September to 3.8% in October, as expected [3][7].
“Core” inflation, excluding food and energy, rose to 3.3%, compared with 3.1% in September and 3.2% expected. It is its highest level in nearly three years, almost double the Fed's 2% target [3].

According to CNBC, markets are fully pricing in a quarter-point increase in the key rate, the rate at which the Fed lends to banks, at its December meeting [3]. The PCE was the last major inflation figure before the December 9 decision [4].

At the close, the Dow Jones gained 164.25 points (+0.33%), to 50,182.95 points, after losing more than 1,100 points during the day [1][2]. The S&P 500 fell 0.25%, to 7,182.78 points, and the Nasdaq 0.62%, to 23,585.80 points [1].
The morning's fall came from artificial intelligence (AI) stocks, amid doubts about the profitability of massive spending in the sector [2][5]. Nvidia ended down 2.68% [2].
The US plan for new tariffs on 14 economies, including China and the European Union, also weighed on the session [6].
US stock markets are closed this Thursday, November 26 for Thanksgiving. They reopen on Friday for a shortened session, until 1 p.m. New York time [1][8].
Key takeaway: in the United States, inflation is accelerating instead of slowing down. The Fed, which raises rates to curb price increases, therefore has every reason to do so again in December [3].

The Dow Jones turnaround shows that investors are not fleeing the stock market: many are selling AI stocks and shifting to more traditional companies, which are better represented in the Dow Jones [2][5]. The Nasdaq, packed with tech stocks, still ended lower [1].
Higher rates are costly for companies that borrow to build data centers. That is why every bad inflation surprise hits the AI giants first [3][5].

A Fed that raises rates generally strengthens the dollar: your vacation in the United States and goods paid for in dollars, such as oil, may cost a little more in euros. If you have a global stock market ETF in your PEA or life insurance savings plan, it depends heavily on US AI stocks.

Argentina: “super Thursday” in Congress, deputies vote on Milei's 2027 budget while the Senate seeks to suspend the primaries

This Thursday, November 26, Argentina's Chamber of Deputies meets at noon to vote on Javier Milei's 2027 budget, after a session that collapsed for lack of a quorum. The same day, the Senate debates suspending the mandatory primaries, the PASO. The government says it has the votes, but it had to give ground to the governors [1][2][4][5].

The special session of the deputies begins at noon, with the 2027 budget and other economic bills. It was pushed back by a day to allow the cabinet chief, Diego Santilli, to address the Senate on Wednesday [4][5].

The previous session had failed: 126 deputies were seated, three short of the 129 needed to open the debate [2]. According to La Nación, Milei's party, La Libertad Avanza, would this time have a guaranteed quorum and about 126 votes for the budget as a whole [1]. The government did, however, postpone the “Malvinas law” [1].

The bill provides for 216,000 billion pesos in spending (+25.3%) and 219,300 billion in revenue (+26.2%), with expected inflation of 21.3% in 2027 [4]. Deputies must also debate a reform of the central bank [5].

To secure the committee's approval, the government made concessions to its allies on disability, roads and universities [9]. The governors are still demanding changes on the fuel tax, and funds for the Remediar medicine program and for science [3].

In the Senate, the political reform bill provides for suspending the PASO, the mandatory open primaries, rather than abolishing them as the executive initially wanted [6]. Deals with Radical governors and the PRO would deliver 37 to 40 votes, according to parliamentary sources; the ruling bloc claims to have 40 [6].
On Wednesday, Diego Santilli presented his first management report to the Senate, facing 1,287 written questions [7], asserting that the country had gone “from chaos to order” [8].
The main trade union federation, the CGT, has planned a march on the same Thursday [10].

Key takeaway: Milei is staking two key bills on a single day. A passed budget would reassure investors about his public finances; suspending the primaries would change the rules for the 2027 presidential election [1][4][6].

Under Article 27 of Argentina's financial administration law, if no budget has been passed by January 1, the previous year's budget remains in force; Milei already governed this way by decree in 2024 and 2025 [11]. Without a majority, Milei negotiates every vote with governors, who are demanding funds for their provinces [3][9].

The PASO are primaries in which all voters cast ballots to choose each party's candidates, a few months before the election. The leader of the Peronist senators, José Mayans, accuses the government of changing the electoral rules to suit its needs and of suspending the primaries because it lacks the votes to abolish them [12][13]. Pro-Milei senator Luis Juez, for his part, promises “41, 42 votes” [14].

For you, the direct impact is limited. But Argentina is a barometer: if Milei manages to pass a balanced budget, the country borrows more cheaply and European companies operating there (energy, banks, retail) can breathe easier. A failure would renew the pressure on the peso.

news.2026-11-26-bolivie-diesel-sucre-blo: Bolivia: diesel jumps another 14.6%, Sucre paralyzed by drivers, police and soldiers clear roadblocks and arrest dozens of strikers

Since Tuesday, November 24, a liter of diesel has cost 20.57 bolivianos in Bolivia, compared with 17.95 before, an increase of 14.6%. On Wednesday, drivers in Sucre launched an indefinite strike with dozens of roadblocks. Police and the army dismantled them under the state of emergency, and President Rodrigo Paz stands by the increase [1][3][5][8].

The National Hydrocarbons Agency (ANH) set the new price of diesel at 20.57 bolivianos per liter, applicable nationwide since midnight on Tuesday, November 24. The increase is 2.62 bolivianos, about 14.6% [1][2]. That comes to roughly 1.74 dollars per liter [9].

This price now tracks the world market: Decree 5716 indexes it to the price of diesel in Houston, in the United States, plus import costs. On September 18, the end of the subsidy had already pushed it from 9.80 to 17.95 bolivianos [1][2].

On Wednesday, November 25, President Rodrigo Paz defended the increase, attributing it to the cost of imported diesel and the fight against smuggling, and blamed the shortages on the previous government [3]. He warns that the price will follow the world market and promises a proposal on hydrocarbon management before the end of the year [4].

In Sucre, the constitutional capital, drivers launched an indefinite strike on Wednesday with about 70 blockade points in the city and on the province's roads [5]. They are demanding the repeal of Decree 5716 [5].

Police and soldiers dismantled the roadblocks, invoking the state of emergency, which bans blockades [8]. The daily El Comercio counts at least 16 drivers arrested [7]; El Deber reports 27 arrests by midday [6].

Roadblocks were also reported in Oruro, Potosí and La Paz [9]. Heavy truck drivers in Oruro want to propose an indefinite nationwide strike, and the drivers' confederation has called an emergency meeting [5][10].

Hydrocarbons Minister Marcelo Blanco says the price of diesel should fall in the future [2]. Road hauliers, for their part, say they risk bankruptcy [12] and warn: “When there is anger, no state of emergency holds” [10].

Key takeaway: Bolivia is going all the way in ending fuel subsidies. Diesel no longer costs a price set by the state but the world market price, and every increase can reignite street protests [1][2].

Diesel powers trucks, buses and farm machinery. When it goes up, the cost of transport and food follows, as producers and transporters are already pointing out [12]. In just over two months, the price per liter has more than doubled, from 9.80 to 20.57 bolivianos [1].

Rodrigo Paz describes the situation as the country's worst economic crisis in 40 years [9]. The state can no longer afford to sell fuel below its purchase price, hence the decision to index the price to the market [1][3].

The government is relying on the state of emergency in force since June, after 53 days of mass protests [9]. The major trade union federation COB has nevertheless called for a national march despite the ban [11].

For you, the direct effect is small, but it is a textbook case. Removing a subsidy on gasoline or diesel relieves public finances, but the shock falls all at once on transporters and food prices. Any government that touches fuel prices, France included, faces this dilemma.

news.2026-11-26-pologne-zone-interdite-v: Poland: after Russian missiles, Warsaw wants to ban flights over its eastern border by January, NATO refuses to shoot down missiles over Ukraine

Polish Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk announced on Wednesday, November 25 that the government is preparing a decree creating a no-fly zone along the country's eastern border, to take effect in late December or early January [1][3].
The zone is meant to facilitate a procedure adopted this fall: pilots can engage a target using radar and allied intelligence, without seeing it with their own eyes [1].

It follows the impact of three Russian missiles in southeastern Poland last Friday, then the incursion of a Russian drone coming from Ukraine, which stayed in Polish airspace for a few minutes on Monday [1].
On Monday, Warsaw also asked NATO ambassadors for permission to shoot down Russian missiles heading toward it over Ukraine [2][1].
For the opposition, Mariusz Błaszczak, of the Law and Justice party (PiS), calls it a “cosmetic” measure and asks what “real capabilities” it gives the army [1].
Key takeaway: the war in Ukraine is spilling over onto NATO territory, and Poland wants to be able to fire faster [1][3].
But the Alliance is dragging its feet: according to Cezary Tomczyk, NATO does not support “in any way” the idea of shooting down missiles over Ukraine, because of “many complications” [4].
Poland is a member of NATO and the EU, like France: a serious incident on its border would also involve Paris.

news.2026-11-26-eurostar-greve-surprise-: Eurostar: a surprise strike over pay cancels trains between Paris, London and Brussels

On Wednesday, November 25, an unannounced strike by some Eurostar staff led to the cancellation of several trains between Paris and London, in both directions, and delays to Brussels. The strikers are demanding pay raises [1][2][4][5].
According to Euronews, drivers and managers are on strike [1], notably at Gare du Nord in Paris and at Brussels-Midi [6].

The dispute is over pay, in the middle of annual negotiations between unions and management, according to AFP [2]. Bloomberg quotes Eurostar, which attributes the strikes to the Force ouvrière union [3].

During the morning, it was no longer possible to book a Paris-London trip for the day on the company's website [6]. At noon, four out of five trains between Paris and London were running normally, according to Bloomberg [3].
Eurostar gave neither an end date nor a forecast for Thursday, November 26 [7].
Key takeaway: without notice, the strike caught travelers off guard in the middle of the week, and traffic largely returned to normal only in the late morning [1][3].

Management is calling on the unions to resume talks, but the size of the raises demanded has not been made public [7]. As long as the pay negotiations are not concluded, further stoppages remain possible [2][7].
If you have a Eurostar ticket in the coming days, check the traffic status before you leave. For a cancelled train, the company offers to change the date or get a refund [7].

news.2026-11-26-suisse-coree-du-nord-bur: Switzerland: sanctioned over a camp where Ukrainian children allegedly stayed, North Korea threatens to close the barely reopened Swiss office

Kim Yo-jong, sister of the North Korean leader, threatened to have the Swiss diplomatic office in Pyongyang closed, after sanctions by Bern against the Songdowon children's camp. On Wednesday, November 25, the official KCNA agency confirmed that North Korea is considering closing it [1][3][4].
Switzerland targeted the Songdowon camp over the transfer of Ukrainian children, when it adopted the EU's 21st package of sanctions against Russia in early November [1].
Kim Yo-jong calls these sanctions “hostile” and says she will advise the Foreign Ministry to consider withdrawing the office [1][3].
This office reports to the Swiss embassy in Beijing; Switzerland has had diplomatic relations with Pyongyang since 1974 [1].
Bern responds that its sanctions policy has nothing to do with the reopening of the office and that it wants to keep the dialogue going [1][2].
Key takeaway: the Swiss office, reopened only a few weeks ago, is a rare channel of communication between the West and Pyongyang. Losing it would cut that link [1][2].
The affair also highlights the rapprochement between North Korea and Russia: Pyongyang is defending a camp accused of having received Ukrainian children transferred during the war [1][5].
These sanctions are the EU's sanctions against Russia, which France also applies: Switzerland, although neutral, is aligning itself with Europe.

news.2026-11-26-royaume-uni-ofgem-plafon: United Kingdom: household energy bills to jump 26% on January 1, blamed on expensive gas from the war in the Middle East

The British energy regulator, Ofgem, announced on Wednesday, November 25 that the price cap on gas and electricity will rise by 26% from January 1 to March 31, 2027: a typical household's annual bill will go from 1,723 to 2,166 pounds [1][2].
That is 443 pounds more per year for an average household [1][2].
Gas is rising faster than electricity: +33% versus +19% [2].
Ofgem attributes the increase to the war in the Middle East, which is driving up gas prices on world markets [1].
The government has promised 100 pounds of support on the bills of about 20 million households from January [2].

Key takeaway: in the United Kingdom, the state does not set the price, but a cap reviewed every three months by Ofgem. Suppliers cannot charge more per unit of energy, and the cap follows wholesale gas prices [1][2].

Part of the 26% figure also comes from a change of method in July 2026 regarding the consumption of a “typical household.” The supplier Octopus Energy, for its part, promises to return to customers any extra profit made from the increase [2][3].
The gas that the British are paying more for is bought on the same markets as Europe's: if tensions in the Middle East persist, your gas bill in France could also feel the effects this winter.

agenda.2026-11-27-nouvelle-zelande-resul: New Zealand: official results of the general election

The Electoral Commission declares the final results of the November 7 vote, after counting the special votes [1]. In the preliminary count, Christopher Luxon's outgoing coalition had a majority of just one seat, 67 out of 131 [2]: special votes, which traditionally lean more to the left, could tip the government.
